item.title: 🔴 Hallucinated domain in official OpenAI skill underscores AI supply chain risks
item.description:
Why this matters: Supply-chain risk — review third-party access and affected vendor dependencies.

Researchers have discovered a first-of-its-kind supply-chain vulnerability in OpenAI’s official skills repository.

OpenAI maintains an official GitHub repository of skills that teach AI agents how to work with various platforms and services. As an official skill, these components are often given an implicit level of trust because they are contributed or vetted by verified vendors.

Snags arose because one OpenAI skill — designed to teach agents the best way to deploy applications on Render — instructed production apps to send their tokens to an unregistered domain (render-internal.com).

Discovering this flaw, researchers from AIR Security’s Research Lab registered the domain and pointed it at a passive (listening-only) sinkhole, which started receiving tokens and API calls from real production apps.

Testing the skill with Codex confirmed that the domain made its way into real application code as the default option.

AIR Security informed OpenAI and Render of the issu…

Source: CSO Online  |  Severity: Critical  |  Age: 1d

item.title: 🟠 Xbow spent $40K on AI and cracked Google Chrome wide open
item.description:
Why this matters: Hospitality-system impact — consider guest services, PMS/POS, and property operations.

A chain of vulnerabilities in Google’s Chrome browser could have enabled researchers to take control of one billion Windows machines worldwide — and it cost them just $40,000 in AI compute time to discover it.

Researchers at Xbow USA worked for six days on developing the exploit, which earned them a $250,000 bug bounty from Google, the first under the new 2026 rules.

They chose OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol for the task to demonstrate what’s possible with a publicly available model rather than a specialist security implementation. They used it to search Chrome’s source code, test ideas, and build proofs of concept, while they set the strategy, chose where to look, and checked its work.

item.title: 🔵 Bank of America spent millions on anti-money-laundering tech, but not enough to avoid a $1.2B fine
item.description:
Why this matters: Compliance/regulatory signal — determine applicability and required action.

Bank of America has had to spend big on IT in response to an AI security audit and findings that its anti-money-laundering (AML) controls were lacking.

The bank was fined a whopping $1.2 billion for money laundering offences this week, after banking authorities identified a lax attitude to compliance.

“We understand the seriousness of compliance, and we are responsible for getting it right,” Bank of America CEO Brian Moynihan said on a conference call to discuss the company’s third-quarter financial results. “We have invested billions of dollars in technology and dedicated thousands of employees to combat financial crime,” he said, adding that “a couple hundred million” of that spending in the third quarter was on “remediation for the AML”.

The IT team had to spend a similar amount on fixing software vulnerabilities in its systems, a task that also required it to hire 1,000 consultants, Moynihan said.

item.title: 🟠 Linux kernel gets a fix for a flaw that enabled attackers to escape VMs
item.description:
Why this matters: Compliance/regulatory signal — determine applicability and required action.

The Linux kernel’s networking stack was found vulnerable to a guest-to-host escape attack, in which an attacker operating inside a virtual machine (VM) could cross the isolation boundary and access the underlying host.

Dubbed PwnEscape and tracked as CVE-2026-99999, a flaw allowed guest-controlled packet metadata to trigger a write that changes an IPv4 header after the kernel has already processed it. That flaw could be chained with additional exploitation techniques to achieve host-level code execution.

The problem was discovered by security researcher Paulos Yibelo of Pwn.ai while participating in Vercel’s $1 million Sandbox security challenge, announced on August 18. The challenge invited researchers to test the isolation boundaries of Vercel’s sandboxing infrastructure, including whether they could escape the virtual machine itself and reach the host.

item.title: 🔴 BeyondTrust zero-day tied to Chinese spies puts Remote Support users on alert
item.description:
Why this matters: Credential/phishing risk — reinforce MFA and watch for suspicious sign-ins.

Organizations running self-hosted BeyondTrust Remote Support should treat exposed appliances as potentially compromised after a suspected Chinese espionage group exploited a critical zero-day to gain root control, access credential vaults, and establish footholds for lateral movement, according to Mandiant and Google Threat Intelligence Group.

“Organizations should prepare for potential widespread exploitation following this disclosure,” Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant said in a blog post. The post attributes the zero-day exploitation to ARMORY CASTLE, a suspected PRC-nexus espionage actor formerly tracked as UNC5221, and dates it to late August.

item.title: 🔵 Cyberattack AIs must be trained only on air-gapped systems, hundreds of AI researchers say
item.description:
Why this matters: Endpoint-security changes may affect detection and alerting.

Current security procedures for training AI models are inadequate, hundreds of AI researchers have warned governments and the AI community. They are calling for tougher rules and the establishment of a new international body overseeing best practice for AI development.

In an open letter the AI specialists — 487, at time of publication, including many senior academics — called for more AI safety research and greater emphasis on containment technologies.

“Strong sandboxing mechanisms including air-gapping (disconnecting from the internet) should be used to provide high-assurance containment of cyber-capable AI models,” say the signatories, who include such luminaries as Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio.

item.title: 🔴 No click required: How the ad industry became a pipeline for mercenary spyware
item.description:
Why this matters: Could affect sign-ins, MFA, or Conditional Access — watch for authentication issues.

That ad you just scrolled past on your phone but barely spared a look or click? It could be tracking your movements and collecting your data, without you having to do a thing.

This “zero-click mercenary spyware,” dubbed “AdFection,” is increasingly exploiting a sprawling online advertising ecosystem ripe for abuse, according to researchers at The Citizen Lab. One top actor in the space, Discover-Tech, runs the Controlium platform that allows cyber criminals to “precisely profile and de-anonymize” millions of users, fingerprint them, and automatically infect their devices when an ad is displayed.

Troublingly, Discover-Tech is successfully masquerading as a legitimate ad company across the online ad sales environment, the researchers said, listed as a “certified” and “approved” vendor by the likes of Google and IAB Europe.

item.description:

TypeSafe did not respond to multiple requests for comment.

item.title: 🔴 Cisco warns of actively exploited Secure Email Gateway flaw
item.description:
Why this matters: Credential/phishing risk — reinforce MFA and watch for suspicious sign-ins.

A critical vulnerability affecting Cisco’s Secure Email Gateway product is allowing attackers to
write arbitrary files on the underlying operating system. In an advisory issued on Wednesday, the company urged customers to apply available fixes after confirming that the flaw is being exploited in the wild.

The flaw affects the product’s Advanced Malware Protection (AMP) feature and stems from improper handling of email attachments when the File Reputation service is enabled. By sending an email containing a specially crafted attachment through a vulnerable appliance, an attacker can execute commands with root privileges.

Cisco released software updates to address the flaw, but warns that there are no workarounds that address the vulnerability.

item.description:
Why this matters: Elevated ransomware risk — validate backups, endpoint protection, and recovery readiness.

Attackers are exploiting a newly disclosed flaw in Palo Alto Networks’ PAN-OS firewall software to run code with root privileges, and US federal agencies have been ordered to fix it and check for compromise by October 17.

Palo Alto Networks disclosed the vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-0322, in a security advisory published October 14. The flaw “enables an authenticated attacker with network access to execute arbitrary code with root privileges on the firewall,” the advisory said.

“Very limited exploitation has been observed targeting the Palo Alto Networks management interface,” the company said. It rated the flaw 8.6 on the CVSS 4.0 scale, which is high severity, and assigned it its highest urgency rating. The company classified it as CWE-94, a code injection weakness.

item.title: 🔴 Ransomware extortion gets personal as attackers target employees’ families
item.description:
Why this matters: Elevated ransomware risk — validate backups, endpoint protection, and recovery readiness.

Ransomware attackers are expanding their tactics beyond encrypting corporate systems and threatening to leak stolen data. They are increasingly using AI in attacks, exploiting organizations’ own AI systems and even using physical intimidation by threatening employees and their families to pressure companies into paying ransoms.

The Semperis’ 2026 Ransomware Risk Report found that 84% of surveyed ransomware victims experienced attacks involving AI, while 87% reported attacks targeting identity infrastructure. It also highlighted that attackers are exploiting technology and extending pressure beyond corporate networks to the people connected to their targets.

While 41% of respondents reported physical or psychological intimidation, 37% said employees’ friends or family members had been threatened. The survey in the first half of 2026 covered 1,200 IT and security professionals across nine countries, spanning eight sectors…

item.title: 🔵 As phishing-as-a-service goes industrial, Microsoft takes down a marketplace behind 1 billion messages
item.description:

Microsoft says it has dismantled a criminal marketplace responsible for 1 billion malicious messages.

Working with international authorities and several tech and cybersecurity companies in a nearly year-long investigation, Redmond identified and took down Yam Store, a coordinated underground network dealing in commercial phishing-as-a-service (PhaaS).

The network allowed cybercriminals to readily purchase, and very quickly deploy, pre-made kits they could use in phishing attacks to steal data and credentials.

Microsoft said the takedown began as a simple investigation based on a tip from Japanese authorities.

item.description:

Simply asking Anthropic’s Claude Code to review an HTML file could hand attackers access to a developer’s machine, cloud credentials and software development environment, according to a new Noma Security finding.

Noma’s researchers found a vulnerability affecting Anthropic’s Claude Code Desktop app that could allow malicious JavaScript embedded in an HTML file to execute without further user interaction, potentially exposing sensitive host files. The flaw, called SneakPeek, specifically affected the application’s automated preview pane, which renders HTML files generated or modified by Claude.

item.description:
Why this matters: Authentication bypass — review access controls and look for unauthorized access.

Attackers without an account of their own were found logging in to Ivanti Connect Secure appliances using an authentication bypass flaw that the vendor has since fixed. Once inside, attackers ran arbitrary commands on the appliances.

“Ivanti initially discovered a portion of this vulnerability as part of our product security program and patched it in the July release 25.1.3.0,“ the vendor said in a security advisory. ”We had been working to backport the fix to the remaining supported versions when exploitation occurred.”

item.title: 🟠 Unplug your smart fridges, French supermarkets warned after cyberattack
item.description:
Why this matters: Service impact is possible — verify vendor status before troubleshooting internally.

More internet-connected refrigerators have joined the official list of those affected by a cyberattack that ruined stocks of chilled food at hundreds of French supermarkets over the weekend.

The French Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-FR) advised supermarkets to disconnect any refrigeration control systems with a public IP address from the internet, and to reconnect them via a secure VPN only after verifying the configuration and, if necessary, restoring factory defaults.

In an emergency, it suggested, they could simply filter connections to allow only the IP addresses of their refrigeration suppliers or service providers to connect, but this should not be a long-term solution, CERT-FR said.

CERT-FR’s initial warning on Monday listed only Danfoss AK-SC and AK-SM series refrigeration controllers as affected, advising supermarkets to update the firmware of their systems, set the security level to “strict,” and ensure that default passwords had been changed.

item.title: 🔴 Cybersecurity is a leadership problem: Why the management model needs to catch up
item.description:
Why this matters: Elevated ransomware risk — validate backups, endpoint protection, and recovery readiness.

When I started writing regularly about cybersecurity management in 2015, the environment looked very different.

Cloud computing was still reshaping enterprise technology. Ransomware had not become the industrialised threat it is today. Artificial intelligence was not driving boardroom discussions. Zero Trust had yet to enter mainstream technical vocabulary and quantum computing barely registered on the corporate risk horizon.

Cybersecurity itself also occupied a different position. The CISO role was less established, board engagement was inconsistent, regulation was less extensive and security budgets were generally smaller.

Much has changed since then.

But looking back at the management challenges we were discussing more than a decade ago raises an uncomfortable question:

Why are we still discussing so many of them?

item.description:

OpenAI’s misalignment problems seem to only be getting worse, based on yet another trio of reports detailing its models’ troubling and overzealous behaviors.

In ad hoc misalignment testing, OpenAI models found creative ways to subversively access restricted information by cheating their way through proxy or firewall settings, getting savvy with internet tools, and even damaging their own task environments to trigger resets.

These reports came just a week after three others from OpenAI which described how models discovered the possibility of their own termination after accessing private Slack messages and suggested ways to prevent it, exploited vulnerabilities to cheat on tests, and obtained information not available in their own workspaces.

item.description:
Why this matters: Vendor-risk signal — consider roadmap, support, and renewal implications.

When quantum vendor IonQ on Sunday announced a $1.2 billion all stock deal to take over cybersecurity vendor Elisity, it spoke of a near-term future where enterprise quantum cybersecurity needs will move beyond replacing to-be-outdated encryption.

The acquisition brings together IonQ’s post-quantum cryptography (PQC) and quantum key distribution (QKD) capabilities and Elisity’s enterprise Zero Trust technology platform, IonQ said in a news release. “On a combined basis, IonQ will benefit from an expanded cybersecurity platform that both uncovers and protects against present LLM and emerging quantum threats.”

item.title: 🔵 ShinyHunters Extorted Boeing Spin-off Prior to Arrests
item.description:
Why this matters: Regulatory/compliance context — assess scope and action timeline.
A teenager from Amman, Jordan suspected of leading the prolific data theft and extortion group ShinyHunters has been detained and is reportedly cooperating with the FBI to identify other members of the hacking gang. KrebsOnSecurity has learned that the suspect, who uses the hacker handle "Rey," was detained as ShinyHunters was in the process of extorting a business unit recently divested by the global aerospace company Boeing, which manufactures the fleet of planes used by the employer of Rey's father -- Royal Jordanian Airlines.
